name: Muna
catalog_quote: 2.5. Stress. With minor exceptions, stress is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, whether it is a root or a derivation. The only exceptions are certain vowel sequences (see 2.6) and words containing the clitic -a (see 9.22). Secondary stress can be heard on the fourth and sixth syllable from the end; stress therefore seems to be spread out…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated place (van den Berg 1989 §2.5 p. 25) in the PDF and text we hold; the cross-referenced exceptions (§2.6 pp. 26-27, ch. 3 pp. 42-43 on clitic -a) were read and are minor/lexical, consistent with 'fixed-strict' penult with alternating secondaries (stress placement coded per word length as 10 010 1010 01010 (1 = a stressed syllable) matches 'secondary stress on the fourth and sixth syllable from the end'). The deciding source is the standard xvi+376 pp reference grammar, the best description Glottolog lists; the author's 2004 southern-dialect sketch (downloaded from ANU, p. 135) independently states 'penultimate stress' for the other dialect. Two open recent phonology papers downloaded are silent. Only un-held candidate is Sidu 1996 (Indonesian, print-only), low priority. sources.quote: p. 25, section 2.5: "With minor exceptions, stress is predictable and therefore non-phonemic. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, whether it is a root or a derivation. The only exceptions are certain vowel sequences (see 2.6) and words containing the clitic -a (see 9.22). Secondary stress can be heard on the fourth and sixth syllable from the end; stress therefore seems to be spread out evenly over the word in rhythmic patterns." Examples on the same page: `ani 'bee'; `bhosu 'w
